extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political economy, social philosophy, and social science methodology
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and methodological rules for conducting sociological inquiry by the inverse-deductive (historical) method: how to derive empirical laws from history and connect them to laws of human nature, and how to combine statical and dynamical analysis of societies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain all relevant facts and assign sufficient causes
rubrics_metrics.description: To apply theoretical speculations to prediction or guidance for any country, one must be able to explain all the mercantile or industrial facts of a general character pertaining to that country's present state; point out causes sufficient to account for all of them, and show good ground for supposing those causes have really existed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you cannot account for present facts by showing sufficient causes, either you lack necessary facts or your theory is insufficient; you must search for missing circumstances or extend/improve the theory. Anti-pattern: drawing conclusions without accounting for known general facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive consistency with past and present
rubrics_metrics.description: A science and knowledge of a particular case render us competent to predict the future only if they would have enabled us to predict the present and the past; any phenomenon that could not have been predicted is a residual requiring further study.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test theories by whether they would have predicted observed past and present phenomena. If not, either (a) look for omitted circumstances in the particular case, or (b) extend the theory. Use this as a verification step before making future predictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish inquiry types: conditional prediction vs laws of social states
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of sociological inquiry: (1) asking what effect will follow from a given cause assuming a certain general social condition, and (2) asking what the laws are that determine those general circumstances themselves (the general Science of Society).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the appropriate method: use conditional, context‑bound causal reasoning for policy-like questions; use historical/generalizing methods to discover laws that shape whole states of society. Avoid conflating the two aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground historical generalizations in laws of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: Never introduce any generalization from history into social science unless sufficient grounds for it can be pointed out in human nature; historical order alone gives at best an empirical law unless connected with psychological/ethological laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require consilience: connect empirical generalizations from history to a priori or independently established laws of human nature. Anti-pattern: treating empirical regularities from limited historical cases as universal laws without such grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification by psychological and ethological laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws suggested by history must be verified by, and connected with, the psychological and ethological laws which govern human action; only then can empirical historical generalizations be elevated to scientific truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use psychological/behavioral theory as a check on historical inference; only persons skilled in these laws can competently prepare materials for historical generalization. Beware of generalizing from history without that verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize limits of a priori deduction for long historical series
rubrics_metrics.description: It is implausible to determine a long series of historical development à priori from elementary laws of human nature because successive generations accumulate influences that compound and amplify small errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to compute long chains of social change from first principles alone; instead use a combination of empirical historical observation and narrower a priori arguments for adjacent cases. Anti-pattern: overconfident, deterministic long-term predictions based solely on abstract principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require sufficient and well-analysed historical instances for empirical laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws from history often rest on very few instances; if even one or two instances are imperfectly known or inadequately analysed, wrong empirical laws are likely to emerge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure comparative analysis uses adequately known, well-analysed cases; exercise caution when the sample of historical instances is small. Prefer multiple independent cases and precise analysis of their elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish uniformities of coexistence and succession (statics vs dynamics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical laws of society are of two kinds: uniformities of coexistence (social statics) and uniformities of succession (social dynamics). Social Statics studies conditions of stability and correlations among contemporaneous social phenomena; Social Dynamics studies laws of progress and sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply statics to infer contemporaneous social conditions from one another; apply dynamics to explain sequences of states over time. Both branches are indispensable and should be used in concert where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze social elements only relatively, considering mutual interdependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Each element of the social state must be considered exclusively relative to all the other elements, due to their mutual interdependence (the 'consensus' of the social organism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid analysing social facts in isolation; infer unknown elements from known ones via their necessary relations. Anti-pattern: treating social elements as independent and expecting simple, one-to-one causal links.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statical inference as provisional substitute for direct observation, with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Social statics can, provisionally, supply the place of direct observation in some cases: by means of necessary relations among aspects of society one can judge of the real condition of elements not directly observable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ statical inferences where direct evidence is lacking, but explicitly estimate limits of variation and avoid overprecision. The exact estimation of variation limits is an indispensable complement to statical theory to prevent error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine statical and dynamical views to derive correspondence laws
rubrics_metrics.description: To obtain better empirical laws, combine the statical view (simultaneous states) with the dynamical (progressive changes) to empirically derive laws of correspondence between simultaneous states and simultaneous changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate contemporaneous correlations and patterns of change to produce more robust empirical generalizations about how elements co-vary and co-evolve.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for the progressive (non-cyclical) character of social change
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat social change as a trajectory or progress rather than a simple recurring cycle; progressiveness means principal social phenomena differ from one generation to the next, though 'progress' need not imply 'improvement'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model social development as directional, recognizing that characteristics of successive generations matter; do not assume periodic recurrence unless evidence supports it. Distinguish progressiveness (change over time) from normative improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites/conditions for stable political society
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain conditions recur in all durable political societies and may be treated as requisites: existence of laws/usages, tribunals and organized force to execute decisions, public authorities whom the community obeys, plus social institutions that foster obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing political stability, check for institutional structures (laws, courts, enforcement) and social supports for obedience. The text further identifies three specific social requisites: (1) systematic education with restraining discipline, (2) a feeling of allegiance or loyalty to some settled permanent element, and (3) a strong principle of cohesion/common sympathy among members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social foundations of political stability: education, allegiance, cohesion
rubrics_metrics.description: Three principal social conditions of permanent political society: (1) a system of education inculcating restraining discipline (training individuals to subordinate personal impulses to society's ends), (2) a feeling of allegiance or loyalty to something settled and permanent in the constitution, and (3) a principle of cohesion or common sympathy (a sense of common interest and belonging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess political systems for these social foundations; absence or relaxation of these (e.g., lax discipline, lack of allegiance, weak cohesion) predicts internal disorganization, civil strife, or fragmentation. Examples and contrasts (ancient commonwealths, Rome, England, South America) illustrate the point.
